systems.title: internal answer engine
systems.subtitle: retrieval over everything the company knows
systems.summary: Our knowledge lived in a wiki nobody trusted, a ticketing system, and three people's heads. I built the thing that answers questions across all of it, with sources attached so you can check its work.
systems.problem: People asked the same questions over and over, got different answers depending on who they asked, and every new hire burned a senior engineer's afternoon for the first month. Search already existed. It just never found anything.
constraints: enterprise data governance — nothing leaves the boundary
mixed sources: prose documents and relational tables
follow-up questions have to keep the thread
every answer cites where it came from, or it doesn't ship
systems.approach: Probe all sources cheaply first, then deep-retrieve only from the ones that look relevant. Rank semantic and lexical scores together, then rerank the shortlist with a cross-encoder. Analytical questions — "how many tools in category X" — get routed to SQL instead, because no amount of document retrieval answers a COUNT.
outcomes: time-to-answer went from minutes of searching to seconds
repeat questions come back from cache
the wiki stopped being the bottleneck
fewer contradictory answers, because there is now one path to an answer
systems.disclosure: The numbers below are indexed against a baseline, not absolute. This is my employer's system and I can't publish real latencies. I'd rather show you the shape than round something up.

challenges.title: querying every source, every time
challenges.problem: Hitting all collections on every request was slow and dragged in noise from sources that had nothing to do with the question.
challenges.solution: Two-stage retrieval. Cheap probe across everything, deep retrieval only where the probe scored. Faster, and the context got cleaner, which mattered more.

challenges.title: semantic search misses exact terms
challenges.problem: Vector search couldn't find an error code. Keyword search couldn't find a concept. Each one failed on the other's queries.
challenges.solution: Run both, fuse the scores. Not clever, but it killed the class of failure where someone pastes an exact string and gets nothing back.

challenges.title: some questions aren't retrieval questions
challenges.problem: "How many X are in category Y" has an exact answer sitting in a table, and a language model asked to read documents will happily guess at it.
challenges.solution: Intent routing. Counting and aggregation go to SQL and come back exact. The model only writes the sentence around the number.

systems.title: ticket automation for field service
systems.subtitle: an automation that survives the platform changing its html
systems.summary: Field techs installing fiber were spending two to three hours a day downloading work orders and filing photos into folders. Now they spend about fifteen minutes checking the machine did it right.
systems.problem: Dozens of work orders a day, each with up to fifty attachments — photos, floor plans, documents — all needing to be pulled down, sorted and tracked by hand. It was the least interesting work in the building and it ate an afternoon.
constraints: the target platform ships UI changes without warning
50+ attachments per ticket over unreliable site wifi
runs take 30+ minutes — people need to see progress
no external api spend; every model runs on our hardware
systems.approach: CSS selectors break every time the platform touches its markup, so I stopped writing them. A local model reads a compressed snapshot of the DOM and proposes a selector by intent — "the download button" — which then gets validated against the live page and cached. YOLO11 sorts the images into FTU photos, drawings, and everything else. Downloads are transactional: all of a ticket's files land, or none of them do.
outcomes: admin time: 2—3 hours a day down to ~15 minutes of oversight
throughput: 10—15 tickets/day by hand to 50+ per hour
no missed attachments — every file captured and classified
one predictable folder structure the techs can navigate on a phone
systems.disclosure: These numbers are real and measured. The classifier is 87% accurate, which means roughly one image in eight lands in the wrong folder — the techs move it and get on with their day.

tables.title: what breaks first if this grows

challenges.title: the platform kept moving the buttons
challenges.problem: Every UI update broke a selector somewhere. This is the number one maintenance cost in browser automation and it never stops.
challenges.solution: Describe intent, not structure. Compress 200KB of DOM down to ~2KB of plausible candidates, have a local model pick one with a confidence score, validate it against the live page before trusting it, cache it for an hour.

challenges.title: asking a model for every click is slow
challenges.problem: A model call per element lookup added one to two seconds per interaction. Multiply by a few hundred interactions and the run stops being worth doing.
challenges.solution: Cache on url pattern + intent + DOM hash, 60-minute TTL. 70—80% hit rate, and average lookup dropped from 1.5s to 0.3s. The cache does most of the work; the model is the fallback.

challenges.title: half-downloaded tickets
challenges.problem: Site wifi drops. A ticket would end up with 30 of its 50 files and nothing to indicate which 20 were missing.
challenges.solution: Transactional commits — a ticket's files all land or none do. SHA256 dedup, SQLite for tracking, exponential backoff over three retries.

challenges.title: nobody trusts a process with no output
challenges.problem: A 30-minute run with a silent terminal is indistinguishable from a hung one, so people kill it and start over.
challenges.solution: WebSocket streaming: percentage, live log lines, per-ticket completions, auto-reconnect. Mostly this exists so people leave it alone while it works.

principles.title: look at the data before you pick the architecture
principles.body: Most retrieval problems I've been handed were data problems wearing a retrieval costume. A week reading what is actually in the corpus beats a month of tuning.

principles.title: boring architecture, interesting problems
principles.body: Postgres and a cache will outlive the framework I would have been excited about. I'd rather spend the novelty budget on the part of the system nobody has solved yet.

principles.title: measure retrieval before you blame the model
principles.body: If the right document never made the shortlist, no prompt fixes that. I check what came back before I touch what generated the answer.

principles.title: build for the second year
principles.body: A demo has one user who knows exactly what to type. Both systems here have run long enough to become someone else's problem on a Friday, and that changes what you build.
